## The idea

Choose a two-voice invention, canon, or contrapuntal excerpt whose lines can be
followed both separately and together. The project asks your representation to
preserve those two views. Each voice needs its own events, measure references,
phrase or motive labels, and uncertainty markers; combined playback must then
reproduce the source's vertical coordination. Revisit the independent-voice
model in
[Lesson 47](../10-texture-and-arrangement/47-independent-voices.qmd) and the
entry-delay analysis in
[Lesson 51](../10-texture-and-arrangement/51-canon-imitation.qmd) first. The
capstone combines those concurrency decisions with the source checks from Part
9.

Polyphonic transcription adds vertical evidence to the horizontal work of
following a melody. A pitch may be correct within its own line yet enter too
early against the other voice, changing the interval and implied harmony. Check
bar totals within each voice first. Then compare their shared boundaries and
inspect the vertical interval created whenever either line attacks.

Annotations for motives, imitative entries, cadences, and implied harmony help
connect those two views. They are analytical claims about the events, not
instructions for changing them. Keep the labels beside the score so a reader
can review the interpretation while playback continues to depend on pitch and
time alone.

## Run this

The model gives each voice an independent eight-beat array. Motive labels reveal
where subject material passes between the lines, and a final alignment check
confirms that the two horizontal sequences agree on the end of the excerpt.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 86

upper = [
  {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 62, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 64, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 67, start: 4.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :answer},
  {note: 65, start: 5.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :answer},
  {note: 64, start: 6.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :cadence}
]

lower = [
  {note: 48, start: 0.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :support},
  {note: 55, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 57, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 59, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0, motive: :subject},
  {note: 53, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :cadence},
  {note: 48, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, motive: :cadence}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp, pan_position|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      amp: amp,
      pan: pan_position
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
end

upper_end = upper.last[:start] + upper.last[:duration]
lower_end = lower.last[:start] + lower.last[:duration]
raise "voice alignment failure" unless upper_end == lower_end

in_thread { play_events upper, :piano, 0.75, 0.25 }
play_events lower, :pluck, 0.65, -0.25
```

The lower voice begins with longer supporting notes. At beat 2 it takes up a
related rising subject while the upper line proceeds toward its answer and
cadence. Gentle panning helps the ear retain each strand, yet the pan positions
live in the renderer and make no claim about the written score.

## Change one thing

1. Delay only the lower subject events by 0.5 beats while leaving the opening
   support and final cadence fixed. The existing endpoint check still passes,
   which exposes its limit: it cannot detect internal overlap or a displaced
   entry. Add an ordering or overlap check before deciding whether the edit is
   valid.
2. Restore the starts and transpose the lower subject notes upward by twelve
   semitones. Their contour and pitch classes remain recognisable, but the
   lower voice may cross above the upper. Listen for whether your attention
   follows register, timbre, or the established melodic identity after crossing.
3. Restore the register and mute each `play_events` call in turn. The isolated
   voice should still have purposeful attacks, contour, and phrase direction.
   If it sounds like scattered chord filling, return to its event boundaries
   and compare them with the source before adjusting the combined balance.

## Why it works

Independent arrays preserve horizontal identity: you can ask what one voice
does next without filtering a mixed event list. Global starts preserve vertical
alignment: you can ask what the other voice sustains when this attack occurs.
Both representations are necessary because counterpoint is heard along each
line and across the lines at the same time.

An interval report uses straightforward pitch arithmetic. Gather every distinct
attack time, find the note active in each voice, and subtract the lower pitch
from the upper. Reduction with `% 12` reveals interval class, but retaining the
full number shows compound intervals, register, and crossing. A dissonance can
be correct when prepared, placed, and resolved convincingly. The report points
to a relationship that needs analysis; it does not forbid a class of sounds.

Motive labels can attach directly to events like tags. Two entries may share a
subject label even when one is transposed or rhythmically varied. Cadences and
implied harmonies often describe spans rather than single attacks. In a longer
work, a separate annotations array with `:start` and `:duration` can express
those spans more faithfully without duplicating the score.

Automated checks can confirm syntax, metric totals, final alignment, and the
intervals implied by entered pitches. They cannot establish that either voice
matches the page or recording. Loop each part against the source alone, then
compare the combination at exposed entries and cadences. Human listening is the
step that joins independently valid data to the musical claim.

## Take it further

Transcribe at least sixteen bars of two-voice polyphony. Deliver a separate
array for each voice, duration checks for every bar, an automatic final-alignment
check, and precise source coordinates. Annotate motives, imitative entries,
cadences, and implied harmonies at the scope each claim requires. Generate a
vertical interval report at every distinct attack and explain each crossing or
exposed dissonance it flags. Audition the voices separately and together. The
combined rendering should match the source, while either line remains readable,
playable, and musically coherent on its own.
